speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a third motion under Standing Order 43, to present a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I am sure the House will recognize its importance and give unanimous consent. It has to do with prices being offered to lobster fishermen by buyers in the Atlantic region. Prices vary by as much as 150 per cent. This places the fishermen at the mercy of the buyers, who are evidently combining to take advantage of the fishermen.
As the price of $1 per pound being offered in Newfoundland does not even cover the basic costs of the fishermen, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter):

subtopic: PROCEEDINGS IN STANDING COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL RESOURCES AND PUBLIC WORKS
PROCEEDINGS IN STANDING COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL RESOURCES AND PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I gave the House warning yesterday, and of which I gave notice in writing to the Chair earlier this day concerning a matter which culminated yesterday in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
May I say immediately, Mr. Speaker, that I am aware of the procedural difficulties in raising a question of privilege in the House when the incident occurred in a committee. A fairly recent ruling is that of your predecessor given on December 4, 1973. However, Mr. Speaker, this matter concerns the denial of that freedom of speech to which members and witnesses are of ancient right entitled in a committee of this House.
Throughout history, in those states of which this parliament is the present heir, the ultimate ruler has ever reserved to himself-as his prerogative duty-the protection and preservation of the fundamental rights and freedoms upon which the state and the institutions of that state are founded. In such a state, when such rights have been denied by the lesser magistrates, there has always been an appeal to Caesar. If there had not been, we would not be here, nor would this institution exist. A denial of freedom of speech in a committee of this House is so essentially an attack on this House that the matter must transcend the convention that a committee chairman's ruling should be settled in committee and not reported to the House.
A committee report that aborts the truth by suppression of evidence aborts the truth no less when it is presented to this House. I suggest that when a ruling by a committee chairman denies those rights which have been given into your protection on behalf of all members of this House, and this House itself, by Her Majesty, then your duty to intervene to preserve those rights is clear.
I shall read the matter complained of directly from the transcript of the May 8 proceedings of the committee. This ruling was appealed yesterday, and upheld by the committee.
The chairman of the committee is reported to have said, according to the May 8 minutes, the following:
.. . hon. members recall that during our evening meeting yesterday a point of order was raised by the hon. member from Nipissing with regard to the acceptability of a question asked of an official of the National Energy Board by the hon. member from Don Valley.
Then the chairman quoted the question, which reads as follows:
Is it your opinion that you have the authority to answer questions such as: Is it the view of the board, as a result of its studies and analysis that the price of oil in Canada should be equivalent to world prices?
He went on to say:
And at that time I reserved my decision relating to the acceptability of the question. However, I am ready to rule on that point this afternoon. I wish to point out to the hon. member that it has been long the practice of the committees of the House to leave to the judgment of the
Privilege-Mr. Andre
officials of the department to decide whether the question would involve them in controversy over government policy ...

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROCEEDINGS IN STANDING COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL RESOURCES AND PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Order, please. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but two things trouble me. First there is the contradiction involving citation 234. The hon. member has referred in detail to proceedings before the committee. I appreciate that in some way the hon. member may want to raise the possibility of disagreeing with a decision taken in the committee. There is a method by which this can be done. Once the report of the committee is tabled, it becomes subject to a motion for concurrence. If that motion is moved, it becomes a debatable motion. It can be called and, in that way, the hon. member could debate whether proceedings in committee were proper. In that way he could expose the matter for debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-CONTRACTS TO UNIVERSITIES FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
1 and 2. Research and development contracts are awarded by the Department of Supply and Services in accordance with the policy set out in Treasury Board "Guidelines for the Implementation of the Make or Buy Policy Concerning Research and Development Requirements in the Natural SCIENCES" dated January, 1973, a copy of which is available in the Library of Parliament. The Policy as a general principle, all mission-oriented research and development requirements as well as their associated and subsequent contracts for hardware, systems and services are to be acquired from Canadian industry, as defined below, unless it can be conclusively demonstrated by a department that optimum benefit to Canada would be better served by obtaining the research and development requirements from federal government facilities. The anticipated result of the policy will be that Canadian industry, by becoming increasingly aware of the research and development requirements of government, will satisfy more of these requirements and thereby produce increased benefits for Canada through greater stimulation of the innovation process. Definition Canadian Industry means all business organizations located in Canada and incorporated or registered under federal or provincial legislation which are engaged in manufacturing, processing, primary and service industries. This definition includes industrial research institutes jointly operated by groupings of companies in Canadian industry. (While universities and provincial research foundations and councils are not included in this definition and therefore not covered by this particular policy, there is no intent to change the practice of placing research and development with them whenever this is the most effective way of proceeding. Each requirement is carefully considered by the Department of Supply and Services in relation to known potential sources for the particular capabilities required. As in normal procurement, if the capabilities required are more likely to be found in universities, these will be included in the request for proposals and proposals will be assessed in the normal manner. A summary of contracts awarded to universities on behalf of client departments during the period of the question is attached, along with a summary of all research and development contracts placed by the Department of Supply and Services during that period.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to plan the Canadian economy and in particular for the injustice of its current wage and price restraint proposals which discriminate against working Canadians while failing to deal with persistent unemployment and the related need for government investment planning.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last week-end in a speech outside the House the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) suggested that unless the trade union movement in Canada agreed to his program of voluntary restraints, his forthcoming budget would have to be restrictive in nature.
After almost a year of inaction since the election, suddenly we have intimated in concise form what the Minister of Finance sees as our economy's principal problem, its cause and its cure.
Coming hard on the heels of the revelation of the government's price and wage guideline package, it was no surprise to learn that the Minister of Finance thinks there is only one economic issue, and that is inflation; that there is only one cause of this inflation, and that is wage levels; and that there is only one cure other than guidelines, and that is further deflation of the economy.
Rarely has an economic situation been so badly understood. Rarely, except for the incomparable Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), has a minister so deserved to be repudiated by this House. As a time when figures released by his own department clearly show that we are in the middle of a major recession the minister remains traumatized by his own doctrine of restraint. He has not only offered a partial diagnosis of our economic problem by concentrating exclusively on inflation, but in addition

May 14, 1975
The Canadian Economy
he has produced a totally unjust and unworkable scheme to deal with inflation. Such a combination of errors would be laughable if it were not for the sad fact that Canadians have to live with the mess which results.
Consider the guidelines governing inflation. The subtitle of that proposal should read "How we plan to get labour to accept the blame for inflation". The hitch in the minister's scenario proved to be that labour was not prepared to be fooled. While favouring a comprehensive approach to the problems of our economy, labour made it abundantly clear that current proposals were totally unacceptable. Why? Let us consider the minister's proposals to deal with inflation.
First, there is nothing in the program to restrict interest rates, even though the amount of income going to those whose incomes are derived from investments and interest is now at the highest level as a percentage of our gross national product since Statistics Canada began compiling data.
Second, there is nothing in the proposal to guarantee low or average income Canadians that they will actually receive the 8 to 12 per cent increases set out in the guidelines. Are the companies which employ the majority of working Canadians-those who do not belong to a union-going to give their workers what is due them out of the generosity of their hearts? If they do so, it will be the first time in history that it has happened. To believe it possible requires a degree of credulity miles beyond that of the most optimistic of Utopian socialists. Why did the minister not commit the federal government to raising its minimum wage to at least three dollars an hour thus ensuring that at least some low-income Canadians got an increase? Why did he not propose immediate implementation of a minimum income program-such as is advocated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde)?
Third, nothing is contained in the guidelines to increase the supply of housing, or to hold down rents, both of which are essential to a reduction in the price of accommodation, a presently crucial component of the cost of living. Rents are shuffled off to the provinces to deal with, and virtually nothing is said about increasing housing starts. Does the minister not know that, next to food, housing is the most important component of the cost-of-living index?
Fourth, no mention is made of oil prices despite the fact that if the government permits a $2.00 per barrel increase in the price of oil this act alone will wipe out entirely the government's chance of reducing the rate of increase in the cost of living by 2 per cent per year in line with its present objective. A commitment to freeze the price of oil would have achieved the minister's minimal objective without involving the whole country in a tangle of unjust guidelines.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there was nothing effective proposed to hold prices and profits in line. Given the corporate sector's almost infinite capacity to manipulate cost data, and the related ability of multi-national corporations to increase their intra-company prices to their Canadian subsidiaries, it is evident that the price and profit guidelines are totally incapable of being effectively enforced.

The only effective part of the minister's proposals would be that which involves the wage levels of working Canadians. Federal and provincial governments would be expected to enforce the guidelines with respect to their employees. The private sector would also have the moral sanction of a government program to enforce them on their employees. The trade union movement-if it had agreed to the proposals-would be expected to bargain within the framework of the guidelines.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, why any working Canadian should ever accept an anti-inflation policy which restrains him and no one else? I ask the Minister of Finance why he brought forward such a totally unfair proposal? Not only is the anti-inflation aspect of the proposals unfair to ordinary Canadians, but of even greater significance at this time is the total absence of any policy to increase employment.
If some plan to reduce the rate of inflation is desirable- as is accepted in principle by our party-then surely we also require an equivalent commitment to produce jobs for the 800,000 Canadians who need them. I will have more to say about unemployment shortly, Mr. Speaker. But at this point I want simply to stress that the total emphasis of the proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance is on inflation and, more specifically, on what he considers to be wage-induced inflation.
For a number of months now the minister has been trying to convince the Canadian public that in the crime of inflation wages are the culprit. He and others have pointed to wage settlements reached in the last quarter of 1974, citing with misleading regularity the statistic that the average wage settlement for that period was 17.4 per cent. Two conclusions were drawn from this statistic, first, that this was proof that labour was getting more than its share of the economic pie and, second, that Canadians would price themselves out of competition in international markets. I would like now to deal with both points.
First, it is important to note that the 17.4 per cent wage increase figure referred to pertains to no more than 3 per cent of Canadian workers. It was an average of the settlements reached in the last quarter of 1974 by the better organized unions in the larger bargaining units. I stress here that 97 per cent of the Canadian labour force is excluded from the 17.4 per cent statistic. Indeed, 97 per cent of Canadians received substantially less than this increase precisely because the vast majority are either in no union or belong to weak unions. The average wage in Canada for the last quarter of 1974 increased by only 5.4 per cent. And for the first quarter of 1975 average wages increased by only 2.4 per cent, or an annual rate of just under 10 per cent. Why, then, is the minister so preoccupied with wage rates?
The second point to be made is that labour income must be seen in the context of all other sources of income. The Department of Finance, in its economic review issued about a week ago, puts the situation in perspective. During 1974 labour income represented the smallest percentage of the GNP since 1968. At the same time corporate profits were at their highest proportion of the GNP in 25 years- since 1951. Is it not understandable and entirely just, especially given the recent rates of inflation, that labour should get these higher increases to make up for the
May 14, 1975

decline in real income that they have experienced in the last few years? If they are still getting increases of only 10 per cent, as they are for this year, why, I ask again, is the Minister of Finance putting the squeeze on the working people of Canada?
I want now to turn to the Minister of Finance's stated concern that, if wages and salaries keep going as they have been, we will price ourselves out of world markets. I say, with respect, that I think his argument in this case is even weaker than the first argument he has made.
What is the evidence? In 1974 Canada had a lower rate of inflation than any of her trading partners in OECD, with the exception of Germany. The latest OECD figures for March, 1975, show that Canada's price increases are somewhat lower than the average for OECD members. However, the main point that I want to make is that any problems we are experiencing with exports have virtually nothing to do with wage settlements. During the first two months of 1975 we had a drop in exports of manufactured products to the United States of about 2 per cent compared with the same period in 1974. What is important to note, however, is that most of this decline is due to a fall off in automotive exports, and that none of this decline can be attributed in the slightest way to wage settlements in Canada.
During the first two months of 1975 our exports in dollar value of raw materials, which account for about 70 per cent of our exports, were up by 43 per cent over 1974. Most of our raw materials industry is capital intensive, with labour costs therefore playing a small role in the total cost of output. Even if this were not so, international forces well beyond our control or influence determined the world price for iron ore, copper, zinc and so on.
Apart from the United States the only other of our major trading partners where the dollar value of our exports was down for the first two months of 1975 was Japan. I stress that the only one of our other major trading partners, with the exception of the United States, where we have had a decline in exports is Japan. This is due to a decline in the exports of lumber and wood products, which have fallen because of a recession in the sectors of the Japanese economy using these materials. Again, like the decline in automotive exports to the United States, Canadian labour costs have absolutely no bearing on the issue.
So far I have argued, first, that the minister's program of restraint is full of loopholes and is unfair to working Canadians; second, that Canadian wages and salaries are not growing disproportionately compared to other countries; and third, that in terms of our trade problems Canadian wage levels have either had no effect or they are entirely irrelevant. All of this makes me conclude that, on these grounds alone, the Minister of Finance's proposals and their supporting arguments should be rejected outright. However, there is an additional and equally compelling reason, and that is that in his bungling fascination with inflation the minister has ignored the ominous problem of unemployment.
On behalf of my party, in both the throne speech and budget debates last fall, I warned that unless the govern-
The Canadian Economy
ment took immediate corrective action then we would have a major recession on our hands. Again in a special debate in February of this year I urged the minister to bring in a new budget quickly to head off a deepening of the recessionary trends. It is no consolation to look at the unemployment figures which were announced yesterday, which reveal that some 800,000 Canadians are out of work. It is no consolation either to look at the industrial output figures that became available today showing a decline in productivity running at a negative rate of some 11 per cent this year. It is no consolation at all to be able to say, "I told you so".
The decline in output at this rate of 11 per cent has tragic implications for thousands of Canadians. This decline for the third quarter in a row means that we are deeply imbedded in a recession. No amount of evasive talk from the Minister of Finance, no amount of charm or clever answering in the House, will enable Canadians to escape this sad fact. With 800,000 Canadians out of work now, unless the Minister of Finance brings forth an expansionary budget within the next few weeks the situation will worsen in a dramatic way. If he remains preoccupied with his current proposals, a million Canadians-I select the figure with care-could be walking the streets seeking employment next December. The Minister of Finance must admit he has been wrong, and must move quickly to take corrective action.
The new budget must be expansionary, and wherever possible increased expenditure should be aimed at both job creation and at mitigating inflation. These are not, as some would have us believe, mutually contradictory objectives.
Let me make some specific suggestions, Mr. Speaker. First of all housing starts, for example, are down by 40 per cent when compared with the same quarter of last year. The minister should radically revise his target of 210,000 units upwards to 400,000 units. Again I select the 400,000 figure not out of the hat but with care.
To achieve this target the government would have to increase in significant proportions its own expenditures. To make sure that the job is done it should also follow the example of the British Columbia government and go directly into the development business. It should take immediate steps, by changing the Bank Act, to bring down the level of mortgage rates so that average Canadians could afford to buy a house once again. By so acting, I want to stress that no or little inflationary pressure will be put on the economy. Indeed the slack in the lumber industry in New Brunswick, Quebec and British Columbia would experience a recovery, and the 25 per cent now unemployed in the construction industry would once again find jobs. Instead of putting new inflationary pressure on labour and resources, such action in the housing field would simply take men and women off the unemployment lists.
Secondly, we need a reasonable tax reduction restricted to average and low income groups in order to compensate for inflation and to stimulate demand in the economy, which I repeat has ground to a halt.
Thirdly, there should be a public commitment to freeze the price of oil. This would be good both for Canadian consumers and for Canadian industry, and would keep the

I am sure that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) would not want to distort the proposal put forward by the premier of Saskatchewan, which is not the position he just intimated. But I will not be sidetracked, Mr. Speaker.
My fourth point is that the government should raise the federal minimum wage to $3 an hour by at least July 1 of this year, and get the provinces to take corresponding or equivalent action in terms of the provincial minimum wage. Again this would be concrete action that would enable low income Canadians to cope with an inflating economy.
Finally and importantly, what Canada requires in the area of employment is a national development plan that takes fully into account certain short run and long run advantages that we possess as a country, and which other countries do not possess. Potential self-sufficiency in petroleum gives us an immense edge over the industrial countries in the Common Market and over Japan in the immediate situation. Our immense natural resources give us a long run advantage shared by few other nations of the world.
What is required is a decisive expansion of the role played by the federal government in planning and directing the economy. Private investment has fallen off recently, for the perfectly rational capitalist reason that profit expectations have diminished. It would be crazy to invest if you do not expect to make a profit.
The government, in our view, is the only force capable of filling this vacuum in the short run if massive unemployment is to be avoided. In the long run, Mr. Speaker, the selective and strategic use of public investment, public ownership and government expenditure, must be at the core of a national development plan whose ultimate objective is to achieve full employment and hold under control, as far as possible, escalation in the rate of inflation.
We must get beyond the boom and bust cycle, the cyclical nature of the Canadian economy; and only a national economic plan can come close to achieving this kind of objective. Unfortunately only the New Democratic Party is committed to such a policy for Canada. The Liberals in a majority situation, which they have had since last July, are once again demonstrating that they are a party of indifference, unemployment, and inequality, a party wedded to the foolish and unjust economic ideas of the past. We are long overdue for a change.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal primarily with the argu-

ments put forward by the leader of the NDP in the House, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). I understand that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) will be speaking later and I want to apologize to him in advance, because the short notice of the motion has put me in the position where I have commitments later this afternoon which are physically impossible for me to cancel. I do undertake to him that I will read what he has to say and be back here for the vote. If it were the hon. gentleman's motion I would be here to listen to him as well, as I usually make it my practice to listen to him when he speaks because of his position in the House.
The hon member for Oshawa-Whitby concentrated, and he is entitled to his choice, on unemployment. I share his concern in that regard, particularly at current rates. I have said on several occasions, and particularly in my last budget of November, that we have twin problems; we have the problem of unemployment and threatening world recession, as I said in November, and we also have the problem of inflation.
The argument I want to make today, as I have made on several occasions inside and outside the House, is that if in present circumstances we do not solve the problem of inflation and non-competitive prices and costs of production, then we will risk future unemployment in this country, particularly because of the non-competitive posture in which this country will find itself. In other words, it is not an either or situation.
The hon. member has talked about outmoded economic policies, but I suggest he has been dealing with that this afternoon. Unless we solve the problem in respect of costs and prices in this country our problem of unemployment will be rendered severely worse. In other words, it is a precondition to expansion in this economy and employment opportunities, with the fastest growing labour force in the world, that we get ourselves back into the competitive range of prices and costs.
If the hon. member is talking in terms of traditional trade-offs, then I think he is off the point. You will recall that the budget of last November has a different thrust than the budget of the previous May, because it was in response to the deterioration the government then saw in the world economy. I have admitted in the House that we underestimated that deterioration. We underestimated the depth of the recession in the United States, and the depth to which that would bring the world economy.
I said then that the budget was aimed at dealing with the twin problems of inflation and slow growth, and that the first essential action then was action to sustain demand. Of course the budget was an expansionary budget in November.
The major cause, as I have said, of this continuing deterioration of the world economy has been the plunge by the United States into the deepest and most prolonged recession in the history of that country in the post-war period. The United States administration only belatedly recognized that, and switched from a restrictive fiscal and monetary policy to an expansionary policy in early spring. The President turned from a policy of tax increases to a policy of tax cuts. It is only now that the administration and Congress are negotiating what the energy policy is going to be, because at one time it seemed to have been
May 14, 1975

counterproductive with tax cuts and with the fiscal spending program.
Aside from the U.S. economy and the prospects we see for the world economy, and aside from oil and gas pricing and some other factors I have brought to the attention of the House, one of the factors the government and I have to take into account in formulating the next budget is the outcome and the prospects of the long series of discussion and consultations we have been undertaking with various groups in the economy, to which the hon. gentleman's motion is really directed, in an effort to arrive at some mutually agreed course of action, if that is possible. That is a course of action for bringing inflation under control in Canada in a gradual process over a period of three or four years. I suggest a period of three or four years, because we can see that such a period is necessary if we are not going to restrict the economy overly and provoke massive unemployment.
I recognize that in some quarters, particularly some rather close ones across the aisle, this whole endeavour has tended to be dismissed as so much window dressing on the assumption that, and this is in other quarters not shared by the Leader of the Opposition, the problem of inflation is rapidly receding of its own accord.
I do not want to include the Leader of the Opposition in this, because he is aware of the seriousness of the problem, but some feel that the recent trend over the last four months, in which inflation has been running at the annual rate of somewhere between 7 per cent and 7!/2 per cent, now indicates that we have the problem beaten and under control. As I said in Sarnia, I believe this is a very dangerous and mistaken assumption.
The problem of inflation, far from receding, has become more critical for the Canadian economy with every passing month because of the extent to which it increasingly threatens to undermine our competitive position both here in our own markets and abroad in foreign markets.
I have seen it suggested that certain government spokesmen, among them myself, have greatly exaggerated the threat posed to our competitive position by inflation. Indeed this was the argument just put forward this afternoon by the leader of the NDP in this House. He argued, as have others, that the rise in Canadian consumer prices recently has compared favourably with the United States and most other industrial nations, except Germany. He argued, as it has been argued in other places, that the increase in Canadian wages and salaries has also been lower than in most nations other than the United States and Germany. He argued, as it has been argued in other places, that the increases in the prices of Canadian manufactured goods have been moderately less than the increases in the prices of those manufactured goods we import from abroad.
While all these points are valid enough, they fail to take account of the trends and tendencies which this country is now facing, and fail to take account of a number of crucial situations. In every country, and this has been stated by Helmut Schmidt, Chancellor for Germany, to whom the hon. member loves to refer as being in his social democratic fraternity, and by U.S. Secretary of State Simon, who does not quite jibe with the political and economic
The Canadian Economy
philosophy of the hon. gentleman-both of them have said-

speechtext: He belongs to your fraternity.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: He is with you and Dick Nixon.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Now Lome, you don't believe that. Both of them, from different economic and political points of view, have pointed out the risk of the re-appearance of inflation, perhaps in a more virulent form than ever, as the tone of economic activity tends to pick up, if it picks up simultaneously in the major industrialized countries of the world.
For Canada, I believe and submit to Your Honour, this danger is particularly great because of the substantial increases in costs that are now being built and have been built into our economy in the second, third and fourth quarters of 1974 and the first quarter of 1975, as a result of very large increases in wages and salaries. It is quite true that these increases generally have been below the average experienced in Europe and Japan, but that overlooks the fact that the United States is still by far and away our largest customer, our largest market, and we export 65 per cent of everything we produce. In manufactured goods that percentage is even higher.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Most of it is raw materials.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
I am talking about our manufactured and processed goods where the situation is even more critical. The very fact that for a considerable period Canadian wages and salaries have been rising at a very much faster rate than those in the United States should make obvious that our competitive position is being jeopardized.
The hon. gentleman says that the recent figures for the first quarter of 1975, of between 16 per cent and 17 per cent, cover only 3 per cent of the work force, but these are the recent settlements. These are the figures that are setting a trend. The recent figure for the United States- and I know that these figures are not exactly comparable but they are close enough-is 7.8 per cent. I am just saying to the hon. member that if that trend continues then it poses some difficulties for this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: It is a trend for a small percentage of the labour force.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Well, the real danger is down the road when the United States economy recovers against the recession. When the productivity at that stage of the cycle comes up it will experience not only a greater increase in its productivity but a greater unit cost economy than we will have in Canada. I believe the risk, if the present trend continues, is that the inevitable result of such a development will be a substantial widening in the differential of unit-labour costs in Canada compared to those in the United States, and therefore a sharpening deterioration in our competitive position. Now more important is that, as a major trading nation, we have already reason to be concerned about the import-export

picture that has been developing over the past several months.
It is true that the major impulse of the deterioration up until now, although I am advised that the cost of production figures are beginning to be negative insofar as Canada is concerned, has been the deterioration in the American, Japanese and British economies. Those recessionary effects have been the primary impulse in affecting our exports. The cost of production figures are now becoming very relevant.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Would you give us some examples-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
I have half an hour and I have to outline the argument as best I can. The fact of the matter is that the more severe the impact of inflationary pressures is in eroding our competitive position, the more severe will become the problem of unemployment, at a time when unemployment is unacceptably high. I agree fully with the Leader of the New Democratic Party. At a time when our labour force continues to grow at the fastest absolute and comparative rate in the world we simply cannot afford to impede the development of new job opportunities on a massive scale.
In my view, therefore, we have no practical alternative but to do everything we possibly can to break the spiral of inflation. The question is, and the difference of opinion in this House is, how? There are a number of different views. To put the issue in some perspective let me recall that this was a question which confronted us with growing urgency in the fall of last year when it was becoming increasingly apparent that sharply escalating domestic costs and prices were rapidly replacing international forces as a major source of inflationary pressure in this country.
We concluded then that there were only three alternative courses open to the government to deal with the serious threat to Canada's competitive position, both at home and abroad, which is created by the soaring spiral of domestic prices and domestic costs. We could adopt highly restrictive fiscal and monetary policies to curb inflation. We could use the fiscal and monetary tools. We could propose comprehensive mandatory price and wage controls, or we could attempt to work out a mutual understanding among all sectors of the economy in an attempt to gear down fairly and equitably the inflation rate through voluntary means. All these approaches involve hard choices. In fact what is before the country now is a series of unpalatable options. We recognized that each of these presented major problems but we also recognized that we had to make a choice.
Rather than adopting the most strict fiscal and monetary policies, which would have resulted in declining output and rising unemployment, the budget which I brought down in November was aimed at stimulating both output and employment in the least inflationary way possible by reducing taxes. We did not feel that imposition of mandatory controls should be considered then, because of the serious problems they would undoubtedly create. Mandatory controls imposed by government fiat, without the strong backing of the public, stand little chance of achieving even minimal success in controlling inflation. We saw no evidence that the necessary degree of public support would be forthcoming at that time.

By a process of elimination we came to the decision to pursue the third option, that of trying to bring together the various groups in our economy in an effort to work out a mutually agreed plan for scaling down the rate of inflation to a more acceptable level, that would be as effective, fair and equitable as possible. There is nothing easy about it. We are aware of the pitfalls and the frustrations. There is nothing easy about attempting to forge, in a federal state, a mutual understanding to govern the setting of prices and incomes among the various sectors of the economy. We are equally aware, however, that if we did not achieve a mutual understanding, the practical implementation of that understanding, even if we are able to achieve it, from day to day would be difficult, as indeed it would be under a mandatory system.
I submit to Your Honour that if Canadians look squarely at the critical threat confronting this economy and the courses and options open to us in dealing with the threat, they would agree that working together to fight inflation would far better serve their best interests than any of the other alternatives.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party made the allegation that the proposals put before labour, management, the professions and the other sectors of the economy, were unduly weighted against the working man in this country; in other words that they were unduly weighted against labour. I would say to him, and to the House, that the program being developed by the government in an attempt to halt the spiral of costs and prices applies to every sector of the economy and not just to labour. Because wages, salaries and supplementary labour income compose some 70 per cent of Canada's national income it is obvious that they are the most important single element in the income picture. But fairness, equity, and effectiveness just as obviously demand that all other kinds of claims on the national income must also be moderated if we are to bring inflation under control.
The working papers leaked to the press I believe were badly misrepresented and misunderstood. The fact of that leak seriously jeopardized the chances of arriving at an understanding among all sectors of the economy. I am going to summarize the substance of the proposals. Maybe the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) has not read the papers I gave him.
We proposed as discussion papers for a consensus, if that were possible, that all groups would be allowed to gain at least the target rate of the increase in inflation, that is to say, to preserve their real income. If the consumer price increase rose faster than the target rate the groups would be entitled to recover the difference in the second year, and would not be penalized for an underestimation of the target rate. Workers who had fallen behind the average increase in the last two years would be entitled to increases larger than the target rate of the price increase of up to 4 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: How are the unorganized workers to get this?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Lower income workers would be entitled to a minimum increase of $600, and higher salaried groups would be subject to a maximum increase of $2,400. The unorganized worker would be put
May 14, 1975

in a better position, as would pensioners, if we could get this problem of inflation under control.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: That does not answer the question of how they will get the increase.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
And there would be provision made for exceptional cases. Also for selfemployed professionals, professional fees could only be increased by an amount required to improve their net income by a maximum of $2400 available to salaried executives and professionals. In respect of dividends it is true, as I said to the House in reply to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), that we have not yet, either with labour or management, solved the problem of dividends and the question of trading off a fair return to the shareholder, but not excessive and not exceeding the return available to the worker, and still preserve the investment opportunities and enhancement for capital investment of those concerned.
On prices-and these were spelled out with the same detail as wages which is the reason I say that the proper balance was not paid to those two items in the report that was made of those working papers-on prices, first of all the general principle envisaged was that for the first year of the consensus the price increase would be limited to amounts sufficient to cover increases in unit costs; that is all. Where the allocation of costs to products was impractical, the onus would be on the company to comply with the general principle. Wholesalers and retailers would undertake not to increase the mark-ups on various merchandise and, where this was impractical, they would agree not to exceed the percentage gross margins realized during the base period.
In effect profit margins would come down as prices went up, unless volume increased. The general principles were not applicable to the export industries, and the Canadian Labour Congress is concerned about, as am I, and as are the industries, how to get a fair allocation in this area, but it is still under discussion.
In the food area there was no attempt at any time to impose a limitation on food prices at the farm gate or on fish prices at the net. Where food prices are not determined by the market, marketing boards will be expected to meet the intent of the general pricing principle. Processors and distributors, however, would undertake to comply with the general principles.
As for interest rates, the primary rate would be determined by financial markets, but the general pricing principles would apply to rates by banks, trust companies and loan companies.
With regard to rent, the working papers did not make any specific proposals because of the continued discussions with the provinces under whose jurisdiction that lies, and the Canadian Labour Congress officials have indicated that they would like to see the principles inherent in the B.C. program implemented.
Provincial governments are receiving the following proposals: first, new construction would be exempt for five years. Second, increases would be permissible up to the
The Canadian Economy
CPI target. Any increase over the targets would have to be justified by cost increases. In other words, what I am saying is that there was every intent that, if anything happens to be worked out, these discussions can proceed with a possibility of equity that is inherent in the system, and this has been made clear to every sector of the economy, namely, that every sector of the economy will bear an equal share.
The suggestions advanced in the working papers did not constitute a firm set of proposals by the federal government but some suggested approaches to provide a basis for further discussions among the various groups. I said from the beginning that the government did not seek to impose a consensus but to help a consensus evolve. The points put forward in the paper were intended to provide a focus for continuing discussion, and as such they are very much in keeping with the consensus process.
I believe it is quite possible to meet many of the concerns voiced by labour, for instance with respect to rents, dividends, professional fees and the position of the export industries. A number of areas of concern that have been raised depend on the extent to which the provinces are prepared to exercise their influence and authority.
I might note that four Atlantic premiers expressed in a recent communique their readiness to throw their full support behind the program for moderating inflation. We are still exploring the extent to which other provinces are also prepared to do so. That is also part of the difficult and complex process of evolving a consensus in a federal state such as ours.
In the absence of full provincial support and co-operation, many of these concerns could only be met by the establishment of an over-all mandatory federal system of controls. It is the only way, as I said in reply to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), in which we would have constitutional authority to do it under the peace, order and good government clause.
In discussions with various groups, we have made every effort to keep them fully informed on the nature of our discussions with other groups and their positions on different issues.
I recall that on January 22, as found at page of 2055 of Hansard, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby urged me to bring forth a new economic policy, as he said "whose objective is to achieve full employment soon, and at least mitigate the effects of this terrible inflation". He recognized the two problems as being equally important. I want to say to the hon. member that there have been precious few suggestions from the NDP as to how inflation should be brought under control. The traditional position of that party, restated this afternoon, is to advocate the establishment of a government agency empowered to control prices, but to ignore the other side of the coin, namely, wage and salary costs. Both have to be dealt with together if they are to be dealt with at all.
Since wages and salaries make up 70 per cent of the national income, it is perfectly clear that it is simply not possible to moderate inflation unless the rate of wage and salary increases is also moderated and there is some ability to obtain a consensus on this side of the market. The NDP also continues to remain ignorant of the fact-either

May 14, 1975
The Canadian Economy
ignorant or it ignores it-that bringing inflation under control in Canada is an essential prerequisite to re-establishing full employment, however you define employment.
I want to contrast the position taken by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby this afternoon with the position taken by some of his colleagues, including the hon. member for Cambridge-Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) and the premier of Manitoba. I recall that in the House of Commons on December 19, as recorded at page 2399 of Hansard, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby said he thought the Minister of Finance "entirely correct in expressing concern about restraint by those who are very well paid in our society". I am quoting the hon. gentleman's words.
He went on to say:
I think that a very good case can be made, for example, for a program that would impose serious restrictions on the capacity of middle and upper income people to extend their wage levels beyond the cost of living increases in the foreseeable future, while others are much lower in terms of their existing income and must deal with an inflationary economy.
I agree with that, and the bias in favour of the lower income groups was apparent in those proposals.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: There is no guarantee they will get it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby went on to suggest that an approach to organized labour would be justified, involving discussion of wage gains as part of a package that would involve tax reductions for average and low income people and a wealth tax on upper income earners. In other words, he felt our approach was worthwhile and justified, and that as late as December 19.
Although obviously the government will have to consider all its options in coming before parliament in a few weeks with the budget, I believe that through the process of consultation and compromise it should be possible to reach a mutual understanding that will best serve everyone's interests if the will exists to reach such an understanding. I understand the risk involved for certain leaders in the community, but I want to say that it is equally clear that if there is no disposition to do so, then there would be no difficulty in creating insurmountable obstacles to any agreement being arranged.
In every system involving moderation of prices and incomes, whether voluntary or mandatory, there will always be problems. No one will be perfectly satisfied with every aspect of the problem. It is inherent in this type of arrangement or in mandatory controls that there is a type of rough justice that has to be adhered to, and there will always be one group or another that considers itself treated unfairly, or that considers that another has been overly favoured.
I note the contention of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby that the government has no intention of controlling prices. He was quoted in the Globe and Mail of May 7 as saying:
Given the ability of corporations who manipulate cost data, the price control guidelines outlined in the government's proposals are simply not capable of effective enforcement.
He repeated that today in other words. If the NDP leader in the House seriously believes that to be the case, one might fairly conclude that their repeated proposals for

the establishment of a price board of some kind is nothing more than a sham. Presumably the NDP believes that a regulatory agency would be able to prevent such manipulation. Otherwise they would not have harped so long on the need for some type of price review board.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I expect the minister to allow me to make a correction in view of the fact that he interrupted me in a recent debate, and I want to make sure that at least we understand each other clearly if we are going to disagree. My specific reference that he quoted was to the particular mechanism proposed by the government, which was involved in dealing with profits as opposed to the prices review board mechanism. My point was that you can disguise profits in a way that you could not disguise market prices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
I accept that clarification. However, the hon. member did use the words "price control guidelines". In any event, I hope that such a monitoring agency proposed in the discussion papers will be equally capable of doing so.
To bring this to a conclusion-and I thank the House for its indulgence-a process of seeking to develop a consensus on voluntary means of controlling inflation has necessarily been laborious and time consuming. When you are dealing in terms of consultation and in terms of a federal state, and you are trying to bring the various representative elements of an economy together, it takes time and effort. We believe that the time and effort will be well spent if this results in an agreement or an approach that offered some promise of breaking the cost price spiral while at the same time restoring healthy growth of output, employment and real income.
As a result of these consultations we came to the conclusion that any plan that evolved must be flexible enough to make it possible to deal reasonably with exceptional cases. It must make special provision for those at the lower end of the earnings scale in recognition of the fact that they are more adversely affected by inflation than others. It must enable those who have fallen behind the rising cost of living to catch up, and enable all of those who work to keep up with future increases in living costs. It must seek to forestall disproportionate increases at the upper end of the income scale that would result from application of flat, across-the-board percentage hikes.
We recognized that there would, of course, be problems in working out a plan that is totally satisfactory to everyone, but those problems would pale by comparison with the problems that would be created by our failure to work out some form of mutual understanding on prices and incomes.
In any event, the facts as I see them are fairly simple. What it comes down to is that the competitive position of our industries at home and abroad is in danger of being seriously undermined, and the future growth of output, employment, and incomes seriously jeopardized unless inflation is brought under control. Of the three alternatives open to us, voluntary co-operation offers the brightest hope of checking the rising spiral of costs and prices in a way that will best serve the interests of Canadians
May 14, 1975

individually and collectively. If that turns out not to be possible-and the government is going to assess the [DOT] present state of those discussions-then I will have to canvass the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and my colleagues on the options we are to bring before parliament. After we have had thorough discussions in cabinet those options will be brought forward in the budget, or at a time fairly close to or coincidental with the budget.
In any event I am confident that if Canadians face facts at this stage in the economy and weigh the choices and options, they will decide that we are far better off resolving our problems by working together than compounding our problems by working against each other.
I welcome the opportunity that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby has given me to put a few facts on the record to clear up this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the last few minutes that the minister was speaking I had the feeling that I was listening to one of my own speeches, except that it was not as well delivered!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
First of all I want to say that I understand the minister may not be able to remain throughout the debate. He has an emergency on his hands, a hospital case. I hope when he leaves somebody else will come in and occupy one or two of the seats on the front bench and show some interest in this important subject.
I also hope that the minister will understand if I say some things that are fairly firm and pointed when he is not here to hear them. I think he can understand that some of these things will not be said for the first time, and they will be said with some feeling.
I intend to offer an amendment to the motion, Mr. Speaker. I want to say that I do not agree with everything the Leader of the New Democratic Party said, but if by any chance my amendment is not accepted by the House I want to make it clear to the minister that I intend to support the motion as one way of making as clear as I can how much I disapprove of the behaviour of the government in recent months.
It is eight months since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) spoke to the Canadian Club in Vancouver and put the fundamental economic alternatives faced by Canadians in these terms:
One way or another a balance is going to be struck in the allocation of shares of the national income between the various sectors of the economy. We can come together and seek to strike a fair and reasonable balance between such elements as wages, prices and profits through a process of consensus which will make possible continued strong growth of national income to the benefit of us all. Alternatively, we can allow the balance to be determined by the process of prolonged and bitter industrial strife, which could leave everyone considerably worse off by substantially reducing the size of the pie that is available to be shared between us."
It is strange how brightly the light shone for the minister so shortly after the election campaign. How tragic it is that, in the eight intervening months since the minister spoke those words in Vancouver, he and the government have shirked their responsibilities and just let time fritter away in an unconscionable manner. The unavoidable
The Canadian Economy
result of all this fooling around is that for many Canadi-[DOT] ans today the so-called consensus program looks like a sham, and from here at least it looks like it is in a shambles. All through the process there has been too much of an air of gamesmanship-too much secrecy-too little public information and too much confusion, sometimes seeming to be created deliberately. Considering the seriousness of the problems which face Canadians, the government's performance must be vigorously condemned by any member of this House whose concern exceeds partisanship.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us that he was really the one ultimately in charge of designing and selling this program. But I judge that he has tied a can around the neck of the Minister of Finance and is happy to see it rattle away as hard as it can.
Neither the Minister of Finance nor the Prime Minister really lent their own personal weight to the process, although perhaps the Minister of Finance is so deeply involved now that he is trying to swim. They didn't get behind this process as it was supposed to be developed. That was a dead giveaway as to how seriously they were taking it. They suckered a lot of Canadians very successfully during the 1974 election campaign, and it looks as though they have been at it ever since.
It is not hard to look back and see that the government came out of that election victory celebration with a terrible hangover. That is about all it came out with-except a majority, of course.
I think it hoped that things would improve fairly quickly in the American economy, and if it provided some short term stimulus in the November budget, that would tide us over a couple of rough quarters. As for inflation, Mr. Speaker, when you spend two months of an election campaign selling people on the idea that nothing can be done, then for some decent interval at least, if you are a sincere Liberal, obviously you must do precisely that-nothing.
Then we started to hear about the consensus, first from the Minister of Finance shortly after the new parliament met, or even before-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: In the throne speech.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
I think the minister anticipated the throne speech-he was ahead of the Prime Minister on that point. Then we heard about it in the budget and on and on ever since. I think at the outset the minister expected a pretty speedy recovery of the American economy. He expected price inflation to abate, and he generally assessed that the economy could stand a little wage demand inflation as a function of catch-up. I think that was what the government wishfully thought last fall.
As a follow-through to the dishonest position taken by the minister and his colleagues-because everything the minister could see today concerning the dangers to the economy, the damage being done to the ordinary Canadian by inflation, and the threat to our competitive position, was equally apparent to anyone who was willing to look

The Canadian Economy
last July-the government adopted a basically sound idea. It explored the possibility of an incomes policy. Then it took this basically sound proposition and perverted it into something which I guess it hoped would appear to be an immediate anti-inflation program. So a new dishonesty was born, and a worthy concept has been discredited as a result.
An incomes policy approach is a longer term kind of thing that takes a lot of talking about and a lot of time. For months and months we did not know what the Minister of Finance meant when he talked about consensus. He would not tell us. It was something which was too confidential for this House and country. We were not to know about it. Finally he defined the basic elements of what he had in mind. We recognized then that he was talking about an attempt to achieve some form of voluntary incomes policy.
To try to achieve an incomes policy under duress is, of course, a strange way to do business. So, to give the minister and the Prime Minister and associates the benefit of the doubt, one must assume that the use of a longer term incomes policy proposal as a cover for the absence of any effective short-term action to deal with inflation started out simply as a time-buying operation-something to help them "make it through the night." I think that is the way it started.
When the minister presented his budget in November this was very apparent. The budget did nothing, absolutely nothing, to come to grips with inflation. All we got was another smokescreen about consensus. It was a time buying operation.
The minister's forecasts made at the time of the November budget were shot hell west and crooked within a few months. Sad to say, this has not been an infrequent development. Successive ministers of finance have made poor forecasts. The United States economy was not recovering quickly. Our biggest customer was tightening its belt and our balance of payments position was running from bad to worse. At last the outlook was terrifying the Minister of Finance. Unemployment was climbing, productivity falling, labour unrest growing, housing prices and interest rates started going up again, while housing starts, the value of the dollar, and confidence among the Canadian people were on the decline. So then the government suddenly had to put up or shut up on its consensus program. What began as a time-buying game became a game it had to play in earnest.
We have heard some of the most outlandish things since then. Now the minister says he wants voluntary agreement, or else! He holds out a threat. He has said-the program is voluntary, mind you-that he will introduce a restrictive budget to enforce his position if people do not go along. In effect he has said to labour, "If you do not go along with what we suggest, if you do not agree, we shall bring in a highly restrictive budget and then you will see what it is like."
I have a hard time taking all this seriously. I have to believe that it is more than gamesmanship. If the Minister of Finance is serious, the government, surely, is in the role of a hijacker saying, "Go where I want to go or I'll blow us all up." That's what this kind of play really amounts to. There is nothing so simple and innocent here as, "evaluat-
ing the options" or exhausting options. A highly restrictive budget now, Sir, would be the final disgusting act of a sequence of events born in dishonesty, nurtured in complacency, and matured in perversion.
When we saw the document-it is not a proposal; I do not know what it is-we knew then that it had made pretty good sense for the government to hide it. Last Monday, when the details were revealed by the Toronto Star, the minister said that it would be premature to comment on the details. On Tuesday he complained that they must have been "earlier working papers." On Thursday, after a statement by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp), and after it was common knowledge that they were the most up-to-date expression of the government's thinking that was before labour and business, the minister protested against the press report of the documents and said, and I quote, that they "did not fairly reflect the amplitude or totality of the proposition of proposals in discussion." That was his theme again today.
He left the impression that the reports were so distorted that he could not even recognize the documents as they were reported. Yesterday he asserted he had read the final documentation before it was sent out. What pathetic and tortuous evasion! After reading the documents one can say there is no doubt they had been fairly and vividly reported in the press. The fact is, Sir, that last week, after they started to be leaked out in print, the minister was ashamed of the documents. They provided no meaningful basis for a meaningful response from organized labour, and have only incited a sterile exchange of rhetoric.
Some will argue as to whether a voluntary restraint program can work, or be workable. I suggest that if it is to be workable, if it is to be acceptable, it must be comprehensive, and must elicit unanimity from all sectors of the economy. It must be expressed in specifics by the government. The government pretended it was working on this question all during the fall, all during the winter, and all through the spring, and then it laid an egg. This really stretches one's credulity.

A consensus, a recognition of our common responsibilities and an acceptance of the fairness of where we are going, must be the foundation of any effective program to bring inflation under control, while retaining the vitality of our national economy. A sense of common purpose coupled with the will to pursue a common goal surely is something more than an option.
I believe we possess such a spirit in this country, and with a reserve of common sense and determination we can restore the health of our economy. However, our unity is a fragile as well as a valuable commodity, and it is threatened not only by the economic problems we face, but by the conduct of the government at this moment. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party is moving today a no-confidence motion against the Liberal government, pointing out the failure of the latter to plan the national economic to fight not only inflation but also the persistent and uncontrollable rise of the unemployment rate in Canada.
While deploring the fact that the New Democratic Party does not offer any means to remedy the government's negligence and blindness, I must recognize that the greatly perturbed economical and social situation is a direct result of the laziness, and I would even say the inefficiency of the Liberal government, although it is a majority and a strong government. It might well be, Mr. Speaker, because it has a solid majority that things are so bad in Canada, especially in the labour field. This government does not listen anymore to people, it has drifted away from

them; it is administering this country as though Canada belonged to it and without any concern at all for the fears and hopes of the Canadian people. There are, Mr. Speaker, excessive claims from one ocean to another. Others are reasonable. At all events, be they excessive or reasonable, the government is turning a deaf ear.
Mr. Speaker, it is not because the Canadian people provided the Liberals with a strong majority in the last federal election that the latter have the right today to legislate during four years without giving any consideration to the claims of the Canadian people. That is surely a harsh opinion, but why not? That opinion corresponds to what the Canadian people demand: this government told the Canadian people in the Speech from the Throne that inflation would be wrestled to the ground, that unemployment would regress and that the Canadian people would enjoy a good and long period of prosperity.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) repeated that in his November budget. He had forecasted all those good things, those nice promises that can be compared to those that were made during the last election. That is what the Liberals were saying during the last federal election, at the time they were turning down the Progressive Conservative proposal on a price and wage freeze.
The Liberals are bragging when they say that Canadians rejected price and wage freeze during the last election by voting Liberal. If that is true, then it was strickly a negative vote, a vote against Progressive Conservatives and not necessarily for Liberals. If, on the other hand, it was a positive vote, the fact still remains that Canadians sincerely hope for solutions other than price and wage freeze to the serious problems of inflation, unemployment and spiralling prices.
So, Mr. Speaker, no matter how one interprets the vote of the last election which gave the Liberals a strong majority, it must still be recognized that the results after nearly a year of majority Liberal government are yet to be seen and felt. What solutions does this government have to curb inflation? What solutions did the Liberal government take or intend to take to control in one way or another the increase in consumer prices? What are the solutions, Mr. Speaker? The government found a few of them. It decided one day since it was elected to set up a Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration to inquire whether they were making too much profit, whether their demands were exaggerated and whether their influence over the economy created a power parallel to that of the government.
Mr. Speaker, let us not go any further and hope for results that will not be forthcoming from that Commission since, first, that will be another commission whose recommendations will be left gathering dust on shelves, all the more, Mr. Speaker, as the name of one of the members of that Commission is Pierre Nadeau who is president of Petrofina Canada Limited, a large multinational Canadian oil company.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this Commission should not be asked to be more objective than necessary because, it is itself facing the same problem that the one it will investigate. This Government, which wishes also to deal with that problem, appointed another commission, the Meat Marketing Commission. Who is sitting on this Commission which has been mandated to inquire whether unrea-
May 14, 1975

sonable profits are made by middle-men between the producer and the consumer? Its objective is to protect the interest of Canadian consumers in order to avoid abuses in that particular field as we know that today the meat business is extremely important in Canada, especially in so far as the quality of food is concerned. So, who is sitting on this Commission? Who are the investigating commissioners? Representatives or executives of Dominion Stores Limited and executives of Steinberg's Limited.
Again, Mr. Speaker, how could we hope to achieVe positive results and really protect the interest of Canadian consumers when the Commissioners are the very profiteers in the market they are investigating? It is all window-dressing; the government must have plenty of nerve to appoint such commissions as a face-saving move designed to demonstrate to the public its concern for such or such economic sector. But when one sees the resource people used by this government to make investigations, one is allowed to entertain reservations regarding the objectivity of the commissioners, but also of their recommendations, if any.
In his answer to the leader of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), the minister of Finance referred to the working papers prepared by senior civil servants and published in the 7th report of the ad hoc committee; and he suggested that opposition members should read carefully that document which is the first suggestion of a voluntary wages and prices restraint agreement in Canada.
It must be pointed out that the cost of living has increased in every sector of our economy, housing, interest rates, food or production cost. In every case, all the government did was to appoint commissions of inquiry which in my opinion are not trustworthy if you consider the members of those commissions, since the possibility of conflicts of interests has not been discarded.
Moreover, the government was elected and they said on the last election they would wrestle inflation to the ground, try to curb unemployment and try to make way for a fair period of prosperity for Canadians. Like all my colleagues, I heard them make such statements during the last election. The people of Canada trusted this government; they expected efficient solutions, since the ones who were most affected by price increases, by inflation or unemployment are indeed low income people, labourers, farmers.
However, no definite action was taken except for so-called pension escalations, but they had always been part of the budget speeches we heard, either in May 1974 or in November 1974. And we shall probably hear them sing the same song during the next one in May. Proposed fiscal measures are always to the expense of the average taxpayer. The government do not want to interfere directly with the mechanism of prices and salaries. They do not want to impose any rule or any program to the Canadian economy. This government prefers, as a policy, to let things go the way they want to, to make inquiries, to monitor possible abuses. Its economic leadership is superficial in that it does not try to find strong allies to wrestle inflation to the ground, or more efficient tools to stop unemployment.
The Canadian Economy
I have read the working paper which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) referred to in his speech. At page 7, on food prices, a problem which affects most Canadian consumers, it is stated that:
With respect to food prices, it may be stated in general...
And this is a paper by senior officials which is supposed to be the Bible of this new agreement on voluntary restraint which is proposed to us.
... that farmers and fishermen do not have the power to determine the prices at which their products are sold at the farm gate or the fish dock. Thus, the question of restraint does not arise.
This is what we find in the paper written by senior officials and which the Minister of Finance referred to.
What means have we today, if this request for voluntary restraint is not directed to farm producers, be they producers of wheat, meat or any kind of Canadian farm product? Whom is this request of the Minister of Finance directed to? To what extent is this request serious, since senior officials admit that they can do nothing, because, in the area of food, it is not the producers who control prices. If they are not the ones who have to exercise restraint, the middle men or those in charge of marketing will have to.
But marketing is controlled in Canada by Dominion Stores Limited and Steinberg Limited, among others, because they are not the only ones, of course. As I said, these companies have practically a monopoly on the marketing of almost every food product in Canada. They control marketing and probably production. And, Mr. Chairman, they are the direct cause of food prices increases.
However, I have grave doubts that the government will ever dare come to grips with this kind of monopoly or collusion in the Canadian economy or with those profiteering at the expense of both consumers and producers.
The minister called on us to read the document. My colleague for Bellechasse and myself put some questions to him during the question period, concerning the main cause of inflation. That is, the cost of money, the cost of interest charged by the Industrial Development Bank to small businesses, and by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing. The minister answered there was nothing he could do about rising interest rates, because this was controlled either by chartered banks, which are private corporations, or by the Bank of Canada in another sector. More importantly, he could not act because this was an international problem. So here comes the "national Trudeau excuse". Nothing we can do. This government, despite its majority, cannot do anything about the cost of money in Canada. But the governor of the Bank of Canada answers directly to the Minister of Finance.
So the Minister of Finance told us today there was absolutely nothing he could do about interest rates. His working paper he wants us to read, because this is his Bible, shows he will not act. Rather, he passes the buck to labour and employers. He says: "Exercise voluntary restraints, because we ourselves cannot or will not do it". He has no solutions to check inflation and unemployment in Canada. That is why he does not act.
