May 14, 1975
The Canadian Economy
On page 8 of the document we read:
Proposals regarding interest
... that is to say,increases...
-this, of course, comes from the minister's advisers, the ones who devised that consensus scheme-
... in interest rates charged by these institutions . ..
-banking institutions, chartered banks-
... should be justified by increases in the interest rates which they pay and their operating and other expenses. There has been no discussion yet with representatives of financial institutions.
That is the end, Mr. Speaker. The Minister admits in his working paper, which is the basis of a supposedly effective fight against inflation, that there has been no discussion and no contact between his department and the banking institutions concerning the level of interest rates in this fight against inflation.
Mr. Speaker, I say that Canadians would be stupid to agree to this voluntary arrangement contained in the minister's suggestion, without having first of all the Minister's formal undertaking that the same sacrifices will be demanded of the Canadian banking system as those which will be imposed to Canadians, with salary increases as determined on the first page of this paper.
One of the main causes of inflation and unemployment in Canada is our monetary system and money supply. It has been said in the House that there is inflation because there is too much money in circulation. In fact, Mr. Speaker, we understand today, since we have been hearing the older parties talking about money economy, that there is inflation not because there is too much money in circulation, but in fact because there is not enough money, because our money is losing its value, because it is depreciated and because the prices are spiralling and getting out of control.
There is a solution which strikes directly to the heart of the problem. Mr. Speaker, it is a solution that the credi-tistes have been putting forward for a long time and which is called consumer price discount. Today, we complain that what is most expensive and affects the prices most is the production costs. Because of prices and production costs, Canadians are going without commodities or food or else they go into debt to obtain them. Such is the situation for Canadians. If one reviews the Statistics Canada figures, one notes that the rate of indebtedness of Canadians is not only increasing continually but that it is reaching obviously dangerous levels.
However, Mr. Speaker, a Food Prices Review Board brochure entitled "What Price Nutrition?", published in February 1975, states that 52 per cent of Canadian families are going without appropriate or sufficient food and without healthy nutrition, because of the prohibitive price of food products in Canada. According to this publication, their diet lacks vitamins C, iron. This is very interesting, Mr. Speaker. I quote:
The significance of the Board's findings in this report is perhaps best considered in light of the Nutrition Canada Survey which was conducted over a 28-month period ending in December 1972. It found large numbers of Canadians with deficient intakes of key nutrients. Nearly 70 per cent of all women between the ages of 10 and 64, for instances, are not receiving enough iron.

Because of the prices.
More than 50 per cent of all Canadians, with the exception of children under 10 and men between the ages of 20 and 39, have sufficient intakes of calcium. Between 10 and 20 per cent of Canadians do not receive enough Vitamin C. And there are other examples.
Why, Mr. Speaker? Because people must watch their budget instead of concerning themselves with the quality of food products. They feed themselves according to their income. Our feeding habits, our physical health depend on the money available. Inflation has become so serious that not only the livelihood but also the health of Canadians are threatened and jeopardized.
The prospects are none too promising either. The minister said earlier that things will improve, that there is no need to worry or panic because that will be back in order.
I will not read all the article but in volume 7, No. 4, of the magazine entitled Revue de la main-d'oeuvre, Quebec area, second semester of 1974, the prospects are described as follows:
The incidence of the economic slowdown will be probably fraught with consequences for the labour market during 1975; the unemployment rate in Canada should increase substantially because of the anticipated low employment.
Two whole paragraphs are just as encouraging. What an outlook!
As I said, Mr. Speaker, within a year, or six months, the same situation will prevail without any solution being found.
That is why I emphasize this point in order to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and to incite him to consider the Social Credit proposals related to adjusted discount, which is not a price or salary control but simply an adjustment of wages against the price paid. An excessive increase of products is thus avoided, which allows producers to meet the consumers' demand. There is no other solution.
The government lacks the courage to act, it puts the responsibility on employers and on unions, but, for the time being, it has no proposal to put forward.

As the hon. member for the NDP says, that is pretty good stuff, but I would simply suggest that the motion today is an illustration of the fact that presumably there is a bit of a rift in this coalition between the NDP and the Liberal government.
In a second sense, Mr. Speaker, I suggest what we are seeing today is a rift within the NDP caucus itself. Those of us who watch "Canada AM", periodically will recall the words of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), who more or less cleared his soul and told the watching public exactly what was going on within the NDP. He said the fact was that they had lost their purpose and the Liberal party had swung so far to the left, and taken all their ideas, and there was really no future for that party. Therefore I believe that what we have in this motion by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) is an illustration of how he at least wants to demonstrate that there is some difference between the Liberals and the NDP.
In that respect, I am sorry he has framed the motion in this form, because while we on this side in the official opposition have very little faith in the way the government has been conducting the economic affairs of the country, we believe the motion is wrongly worded and implies at least some type of socialistic planning which is so much an integral part of NDP thinking.

As our leader has indicated, and we certainly intend to support his amendment, in order to show our opposition to the government benches we will unfortunately have to vote for the hon. member's motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
The Canadian Economy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) joined in this debate earlier, spending most of his time talking about the consensus program. He stated that one of his alternatives was a highly restrictive fiscal and monetary policy for the country.
This motion before us is really related to the mismanagement of our economy. Surely the government must accept the fact that our present problems can be laid at its doorstep. It is the high government spending and the almost unbelievable increase in the money supply in this country that has contributed more than any other single thing to the inflation we are living with today.
Earlier today I directed a question to the Minister of Finance in which I pointed out that Federal Reserve Chairman Burns in the United States has given a commitment to Congress that he will not increase the money supply in that country by more than 5 per cent to IVi per cent. I asked our Minister of Finance if he had a similar commitment from the Governor of the Bank of Canada to assure that there would be some restraint in this country.
The minister replied, "Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman put this type of question to the House before. Over the whole 12-month period ending March, 1975, the increase in the money supply series has been 12 per cent, M-1,-"there he is referring to the primary money supply system-"a figure which appears to be within the range that is reasonable in the circumstances in terms of the nominal growth of the economy."
Here we have a Minister of Finance telling us that a 12 per cent increase in our money system is reasonable. He failed to point out of course that in the first three months of 1975, the first quarter, the M-1 growth in Canada was 33.1 per cent, compared to a growth in the same quarter in the United States of 4.4 per cent. He also failed to point out that if you review the growth of the money system in the United States and in Canada and compare the two growths, during the period our present Minister of Finance has been in office you will find that our money growth has been almost twice as fast as that in the United States.
Those are the facts. The minister must know this. He fails to level with the Canadian public. Instead he chooses to single out sectors of the economy, such as labour, and blame them for whatever inflationary pressures we now have or which he may feel will occur in the future.
If we turn to the matter of government spending I could give equally alarming figures concerning the growth in federal expenditures under this government. For example, federal government expenditures in 1974 were twice what they were in 1969, three times the amount spent in 1961, or 12 times the 1950 level. Let there be no mistake, that is the fertile ground in which the inflation we are now living with has been planted.
Dealing with this motion and the amendment thereto, I would suggest that first of all we must see how on earth we in this country got into the present position. This is the most fortunate country in the world. We have an alert, growing population, well educated people, and resources that are the envy of the world. We often overlook our good fortune. Canada, with slightly over half of one per cent of

The Canadian Economy
the world's population, has 7.3 per cent of its land surface, 15 per cent of its known fresh water resources, and a disproportionately large percentage of proven and potential reserves of many key minerals including, if you like, the Athabasca tar sands which have potential reserves of oil approximating the total proven conventional reserves of the rest of the world put together.
Similarly we are amongst the world's leading producers of food, grain and livestock. Indeed we have the potential to be self-contained in respect of most vital resources. With such potential one would expect that we could take a significant lead in the world in helping underdeveloped nations and relieving international tensions. At home we would appear to have every ingredient necessary to make our people number one in the world in true wealth, yet we find we are losing, not gaining, relative to other people in the world. Figures recently released show that Canada now is number six in per capita wealth. Imagine! We were number two in the world and we had reason to believe we could be number one, yet under the present Minister of Finance and the present government we have slipped from number two to number six on a per capita basis among the significant countries of the world.
With such a capability in respect of our resources and our people one would expect that poverty would become less and less in this nation. Yet we find the drive to lessen poverty in Canada has made little or no progress in the past 15 years.
I think it is significant to point out that in the previous 200 years significant gains were made in overcoming poverty in this country. If we go back to 1763 we find it is estimated that at that time 95 per cent of the people living in the colonies that are now part of Canada were poor by any standard. By the time of Confederation around 80 per cent were still below the poverty level, but by 1961 those classed as poor in the country were down to approximately 20 per cent. Since then, however, this percentage has remained static-I think this is significant-while the welfare bill in Canada has risen five-fold. In 1975 we will spend more than $22 billion, which is more in real terms than all government spending in 1961. Expressed another way, about 20 per cent of the nation's national income will be used to help relieve those less fortunate, but their plight does not appear to be improving. The modern notion that a state can spend its way out of poverty is not working in Canada.
Surely the time has come when we must seriously ask ourselves why we in Canada appear to be faring so poorly. If one believes the words of the Minister of Finance it would appear that he believes we will do still worse in the future. Why should our real growth now be projected at zero for the current year? In fact under our present Finance Minister we find that not only is our real growth turning to zero but that we have had more unemployment and triple the inflation that we had under former Finance Minister Benson, his predecessor, and we are heading into the highest trade deficit in our history.
Many of us can recall that we complained about Finance Minister Benson, but I can tell you that he was the height of fiscal and monetary responsibility compared to our present Minister of Finance.

I should like to touch on many other points. I would suggest that this government has really been the most permissive government we have ever had in Canada. It will be known as the Permissive Government. It is a government which is permissive on all fronts, not only on the economic front but in respect of law and order. This government has no equal in respect of its permissiveness. Rather than a Just Society they have given us a Permissive Society.
As has often been mentioned, income taxes have risen as a result of the government's action at a much faster rate than real terms would justify. Strikes are becoming an increasing problem; 9.2 million days were lost last year, one of the worst records in the industrial world, compared to 3.9 million days lost in 1969. These are the reasons we believe, in spite of the wording of the present motion, that we must join in condemning the government for the way it has been operating, particularly with respect of the economy. In seven years under our present Prime Minister we have had less real growth than in the previous seven years. Yet there has been three times the inflation, and a higher percentage of our work force unemployed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Why do you not mention the new jobs that have been created?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
At the present time the percentage of our gross national product that i$ going into government is 40 per cent compared to about 30 per cent in 1960. If this government activity fails, I suggest it fails by being too expansive.
Our friends to the left have often stated that they believe that the epitomy of state planning or of their socialized planning approach is Sweden. I suggest to them that Sweden is perhaps a good example of what not to do or, if you like, what to do if you must have a socialist state.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
I would point out that in that state 95 per cent of the economy is still in private hands, in fact more than in Canada. I would also point out that the Swedes are very careful. Instead of interfering with the private sector, certainly by taking it over, they state quite openly that they believe that the private sector must be preserved in order that they can get the tax revenue needed for their welfare programs.
I would simply suggest that this little alliance of the NDP and, if we believe the President of the Treasury Board, the Liberals, who are really slow NDP'ers judging from his words, will lead us more and more into a state intervention system, one in which we will be placed virtually in a situation where our present economy will become worse and worse, partly due to the lack of direction from the government and partly the unfair interference from the government in the operation of our economy.
If we are ever to put an end to spiralling prices, high interest rates and economic stagnation we must stop the growth of government, especially in the commercial field, and we must put our monetary and fiscal house in order. To reverse the trend of fiscal irresponsibility we need
May 14, 1975

stronger leadership in Ottawa. We must resist the current feeling that there must be more and more government spending and government involvement. It is hurting, not helping our progress.
I suggest to my friends to the left that our free enterprise system, for all its faults, has at least made this country prosperous.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: The workers did.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext: But I would also suggest that it is a mile ahead of whatever is running second. Some like to proclaim the inevitability of the demise of this system. I suggest that there is no way in which this system will fall into a demise if we are alert. The fact is that our economic system has raised us from a poverty ridden group of colonies, where 95 per cent of the people were poor by any measure, into a great agricultural and industrial power. We now define poverty in this country at an income level that is higher than the average income level of the world's strongest communist nation, and at a level higher than the average income in 80 per cent of the nations of the world. Yet our government, through its inaction and misdirection, has placed this system in jeopardy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PLAN THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be very interesting to see the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) rise in his seat after his attack on the horrors of socialism and the horror of this party and vote in favour of the motion put forward by this party which calls for more government investment planning. It would be interesting to see him support that motion, as his leader will do, after the speech he has just made.
I must say at the outset that when I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) today I thought for a while I was seeing the ghost of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) of a year or so ago, or of the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) retreaded, because the minister's speech was like a rereading of their speeches.
With the wealth that we have in this country and with our resources it is a real tragedy that we have so much inequality and so many inequities between those who have money and the working people who produce the goods and services.
We have a government that claims it cannot do anything for the fundamental reason that it believes in the so called free enterprise system and free marketplace. Of course that no longer exists because today we have large corporations that make the decisions affecting the lives of every Canadian. We do not have the old free marketplace. The Minister of Finance in that type of situation is like an economic eunuch. He does not have any power whatsoever to guide the economy. The only thing he can do is to point a finger at another scapegoat, and the scapegoat that he has chosen on this occasion is collectively the working people of Canada.
Liberal governments have often chosen scapegoats in the past, and now in the recent statements they made they are attacking the working people who, they say, are responsible, because of their wage demands, for a push in the inflationary spiral. They say that the trade unions are responsible. I disagree. It is a highly irresponsible statement that is far from the truth.
The Canadian Economy
I want to spend a few minutes this afternoon speaking about the government's consensus proposals. I believe these proposals are both misguided and unfair. They are misguided in terms of the entire economy, and they are unfair to the working people from one part of the country to the other. They fail to address themselves to the very serious economic problems. They constitute an economic package that runs the risk of aggravating these problems. We are now in a serious recession in our country. The real gross national product fell by 1.3 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1974. After two quarters of stagnation, today's figures show a 2.8 per cent decline in the industrial output index which, adjusted over a year, represents a drop of some 11 per cent in 1975.
All this makes it very clear that we are now in a very serious recession in Canada, despite the predictions of the Minister of Finance last November when he spoke about a real growth rate of some 4 per cent.
Unemployment at a seasonally adjusted rate was 7.2 per cent in both March and April. We now have the highest unemployment rate of any time since the summer of 1961, and economists are predicting that by the end of this year our unemployment rate is likely to hit 8 per cent, and that perhaps one million Canadian people will be looking for work between Christmas and the succeeding year. Housing starts are down for the first month of this year and are running at about 50 per cent of the rate in 1974.
It is clear that we now need a substantial stimulation of the economy to get it moving again, to build homes, and to provide jobs. Our emphasis in parliament must be to create jobs and to stimulate and expand the economy. In fact the Minister of Finance himself from time to time in the past has recognized the urgency of the problem. He had even recognized the fact that higher output and production, a buoyant economy, in the long run are the best means to combat inflation in this country.
In its speech from the throne on September 30 last the government expressed the view that "higher production, not lower, is essential to slowing down price advances". I wish that it would follow its own advice in the month of May. In the budget of November 18 the Minister of Finance said that "the first essential is action to sustain demand". In a speech to that great workers' club, The Canadian Club of Toronto, on January 27, the minister explained that:
The budget last November-was considerably more expansionary than that in May because of our recognition of the need to offset the economic drag imposed by continuing stagnation abroad.
In the same throne speech the Minister of Finance quoted with approval the review of the C. D. Howe Research Institute, as contained in its "Policy Review and Outlook for 1975," that it is an expanding economy that in time will enable us to grow out of inflation by providing the increase in real purchasing power Canadian families need to meet the increased cost of food and energy.
The Minister of Finance and his advisers said a few months ago that we need an expanding economy and we need to create jobs. But what happened to that analysis in the last few weeks? It disappeared and was replaced by an attempt, subtle and unmistakable, to lay the blame for all

May 14, 1975
The Canadian Economy
the ills of the economy on the Canadian workers for trying to grab more than their fair share of the national income. He tried to convey the idea that the greed of the Canadian workers has threatened to price Canadian business out of international markets. What he failed to tell us is that a year or two ago when we had excessive profits and price increases, it was those factors which were responsible for making our goods less competitive in the marketplace, rather than the wage increases which are still far below what the working people deserve.
Are workers getting more than their fair share? My party maintains they are not. For three years the government has let inflation go hog wild, has permitted prices to rise unchecked, and has let big corporations get away with profiteering. All this has had the effect of seriously eroding the purchasing power of wages and salaries. In real terms and as a proportion of the gross national product, wages have shown a substantial decline in the last few years.
Figures from the Canadian Labour Congress show that average wages and salaries in real terms-in terms of purchasing power-based on 1972 dollars have declined by 2.7 per cent from the fourth quarter of 1972 to the fourth quarter of 1974.
As a percentage of gross national product, wages and salaries dropped to 53.7 per cent in 1974 from a high of 55.1 per cent in 1971. During that same period corporate profits as a percentage of the GNP increased from 9.7 per cent in 1971 to 13.1 per cent in 1974. Where was the Minister of Finance when that happened? Why was he not protesting? He was dining on filet mignon and sipping champagne with his corporate buddies from Toronto's Bay Street- and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). Why is he protesting now when the worker is striving to catch up because of the high profit increases of the corporations?
The Minister of Finance recognized-or in the past pretended to recognize-the merit of the argument I am making. I want to read something he said so that the minister and this parliament can realize the change of mind and heart that he has gone through. In this House on February 28 the minister said:
It is now quite understandable that wage and salary rates are attempting to catch up so as to offer some sort of compensation for the erosion of income ... as a result of rising prices over the last 18 months.
Then in a speech in Montreal on January 29 he said:
Salary demands being voiced by organized labour are not out of step with today's reality. Workers are suffering real losses because of the rise in the consumer price index.
Believe it or not that is what the Minister of Finance said a few months ago, before spring came along and he changed his colour.
In a speech to the first ministers' conference last month, before he mounted the Tory bandwagon, he said:
In many cases, the rise in the cost of living has more than wiped out the benefit an employee expected to gain from the pay increases he has obtained in recent years.
This was the minister just a month ago justifying what we see happening in the economy today. But now, having apparently recognized the justice of the workers' attempt to catch up with rising prices, he tries to do what the hon. member for Don Valley recommended a year ago-to

impose wage controls that will see the workers' income fall further behind, and so he attempts to blame our economic problems on the workers' legitimate demands.
Our party will not tolerate that, Mr. Speaker. Our party represents the working people of this country. Our party stands for the redistribution of income and wealth so that the ordinary working person in this country gets the share that he deserves. He is the person who produces, and he deserves the major of the wealth.
Are our economic problems the result of the greed of Canadian workers? Of course not. Even the Minister of Finance admitted they were not. In his budget speech last November he attributed our economic slowdown to the deteriorating economic performance of the countries to which we export, to the decline in housing starts, and to a number of other factors not related to the Canadian worker. At that time he said:
We believe that the principal threat to the growth of our production and employment comes to us from abroad.
In his speech to the House on March 13 he again expressed the view that our economic slowdown resulted from falling exports that were attributable-not to high wages in Canada-but to serious recessions in the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom-our three largest customers.
Why, in the last few weeks, is the minister blaming the Canadian worker for the slowdown and the inflation in our economy? Again, in that speech to the Canadian Club of Toronto in January, he said:
In 1975, the growth of Canadian output will inevitably fall significantly below potential, primarily because of lagging export sales as a result of economic stagnation abroad and a slowdown in housing construction.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that all the alarmist talk in recent weeks about excessive wage demands threatening to price us out of world markets is nothing short of bunkum. As we say in the farmyard in Saskatchewan, it is nothing short of pure horse fertilizer, and I know the Minister of Finance realizes that. I suggest that he has adopted this tactic of laying blame at the feet of the workers in a cynical and desperate attempt to divert attention from the real problems in our economy and from the fact that he does not have any new solutions for them.
What is the minister now proposing? He is proposing wage and price controls that will not solve any of our real problems but will only exacerbate the injustices and inequities in our society, and that will have no real long term impact on inflation in Canada. He is suggesting this on a voluntary basis, but if they are to work they will have the same negative effect as compulsory controls would have if they were implemented.
The government has cleverly attempted to create the impression that voluntary price and wage controls somehow are different. I maintain they are not different, Mr. Speaker. During the last election the Minister of Finance argued that wage and price controls would not work against imported goods, which represent about one-third of the goods we consume. He was right, of course, and he is right whether controls are compulsory or mandatory. That does not make any difference, and I am sure any economist would agree with me on that.

He also argued that controls have been ineffective in moderating inflation in other countries, and he was prone to point to the experience of the United States or of the Conservative Party in Britain. Why is the minister now trying to reach consensus? If voluntary controls are to work they will have the same effect as mandatory controls, and will cause the same distortion in the economy.
I do not believe that anyone can take what the minister is saying very seriously. He is saying that the working people whose wages are out in the open are the ones who have to toe the line, that they cannot have wage increases any higher than 12 per cent or $2,400 a year, whichever is the lesser. That sort of position will discriminate against the person working as a janitor, or working as a waitress. It will discriminate against the ordinary working person of this country, but not against the man making $20,000 a year, the member of parliament, the judge, the corporate executive, the lawyer, the doctor, or any other professional person earning fees.
The Canadian Economy
developed by the provincial and federal governments. The Canadian people would control their own financial institutions, and decide what is really important for them.
We have to do this if the ordinary citizen is to share more equally in our national wealth. Surely it is the wish of the Canadian people, as it is of the NDP, to establish justice and equality in this country for one and all.

I notice, sadly, although with humour, that the minister forgot to tell us about interest rates. He forgot to talk about dividends, rents, and a number of other forms of income, because he represents the people in our country who get such income. He and the government govern for those people.
